title: Trippa alla Romana
author: Marco Bellini
desc: Tripe simmered slowly in tomato with mint and pecorino, another beloved fixture of Rome's traditional quinto quarto cuisine, mint being the dish's distinctive, unexpected finishing touch.
longDesc: The addition of fresh mint (mentuccia, a wild Roman mint) at the end of cooking is what sets trippa alla Romana apart from tripe preparations elsewhere in Italy, cutting through the richness with a burst of herbal freshness.
ingredients: 1 kg (2.2 lb) pre-cleaned honeycomb tripe, cut into strips
60 ml (¼ cup) extra virgin olive oil
Salt and chili flakes, to taste
steps: Blanch the tripe in a large pot of boiling water for 5 minutes, then drain and rinse.
Warm the olive oil in a clean pot and sauté the onion, carrot, and celery until softened, then add the garlic.
Add the tripe and stir to coat, then pour in the wine and let it reduce.
Add the crushed tomatoes and enough water to just cover, season, and bring to a gentle simmer.
Cover and cook for 1.5–2 hours, until the tripe is very tender, checking occasionally and adding water if needed.
In the final few minutes, stir in a generous amount of fresh mint.
Serve hot in bowls, topped with a generous shower of pecorino.
chefTips: Buy tripe that's already been cleaned and partially pre-cooked by your butcher, which significantly shortens the process.
The fresh mint added at the end is essential to the dish's character — don't substitute dried mint, which lacks the same bright quality.
Like many braises, this improves with a day's rest in the refrigerator.
commonMistakes: Skipping the initial blanch, which helps remove any residual odor from the tripe.
Adding the mint too early, which loses its bright, fresh character over long cooking.
Rushing the braise, which leaves the tripe with an unpleasantly chewy texture.
storage: Refrigerate up to 3 days; flavor improves the next day.
healthBenefits: A good source of protein; tripe is also relatively low in fat compared to other cuts.
culturalNote: Trippa alla Romana is a fixture of Rome's traditional quinto quarto cuisine, historically eaten on Saturdays in the city's working-class trattorie.
